newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AUSTRALIA-TELECOMS-Keen interest in Australia bandwidth.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AUSTRALIA-TELECOMS-Keen interest in Australia bandwidth.

text.p: Strong offshore interest is expected when the Australian government auctions open rights to its radio spectrum next year, the government's Spectrum Management Authority said on Monday.

The government is expected to reap between A$900 million and A$2.4 billion from the 1800 megahertz auctions with wide interest anticipated from established local carriers Telstra Corp, Optus Communications Pty Ltd and the Vodafone Group.

"There's some pretty wild speculation out there in the market place about what this spectrum is worth, but from the SMA's point of view, we really don't know," Spectrum marketing manager Ian Hayne told Reuters in an interview.
"I think the reality there is that we won't know what we're going to get until we actually put it on the block and see who comes."

Industry sources said strong bidding was also likely from offshore telecoms such as New Zealand Telecom, British Telecom and U.S.-based BellSouth Corp as they prepared to enter the post-July 1997 deregulated Australian market.
"This spectrum is all about new telecommunications services and you can expect a lot of people wanting to come in to participate in a more liberal telecommunications market," Hayne said.
"Anyone in the Asian tiger economies, I think, is worth a go as a potential buyer."
He said the auctions were the first in the world where successful bidders would buy the right to use their spectrum bandwidth for any technology.
The Australian system would allow successful bidders to update with technology as it progressed.
"We're combining a modified version of the U.S. auction system with our new ideas about spectrum property rights to come up with a hybrid that is an advance on what the Americans are doing," he said.
In the United States, successful bidders win the right to use the spectrum for a specified technology.
"We're getting indications that the Americans are likely to follow suit," Hayne said.
He said the idea of selling spectrum management will also give buyers the right to sub-divide and on-sell their parts of the spectrum, which will further enhance industry competition.
"That's a major advance and it will help to impose a cost discipline on the SMA," Hayne said.
The first test of the Australian system would come from December 1 when the authority will auction 17 areas in the 500-megahertz band.
The 500 MHz band is generally used for two-way radios and radio-based telephone systems such as that run by Telstra in remote areas.
However, the industry was focussing on the 1800 MHz auctions because of the bandwidth's suitability for mobile telephony including the widely-used European DCS-1800 system.
Optus spokeswoman Kate Van den Broek said the carriers needed more capacity for mobile services as the growth in mobile usage within Australia had been far beyond forecasts.
"We'll buy spectrum to top up, to provide extra capacity for our customers today, because we know we are going to need more capacity later on," she told Reuters.

Hayne said final details of the 1800 MHz auctions would become available early next year with a number of issues still to be finalised, including the possibility of expanding the licence term to 15 years from the current 10 years.
